summary: git restore undoes changes you have not committed. Without options it resets a file to the last commit; with --staged it only unstages the file.
notes: git restore file throws away your edits to that file. Git cannot get them back, because they were never committed.
git restore --staged file is the undo for git add. The file keeps your edits.
git status prints these commands for you under each section, so you do not have to remember them.
pitfall: git restore . resets every changed file in the folder at once. Check git status first so you do not lose work you meant to keep.
setup_note: Starts in a repository with one commit that has gradebook.py, README.md, and scores.csv.
setup:
cat > gradebook.py <<'EOF'
scores = [88, 92, 79, 95]
average = sum(scores) / len(scores)
print("Average:", average)
EOF

cat > README.md <<'EOF'
# Gradebook
Quiz scores for Period 3.
EOF

cat > scores.csv <<'EOF'
name,score
Ava,88
Liam,92
Noah,79
Zoe,95
EOF
